title: Beyond Task Success: Behavioral and Representational Diagnostics for WAM and VLA
action_head: mixed: flow/diffusion action experts (pi0, pi0.5, X-VLA) and video/world-model-based action generation (WAMs)
methods: behavioral metrics: delta/acceleration/jerk, chunk-boundary jump, low-motion failure rate, target-object progress, distractor drift, manipulation-stage completion, runtime
TopK SAEs (with AuxK loss) on last or near-last hidden latents of current-vision, future and action streams per model

weakly supervised labeling of SAE features as memorized / reactive-general / predictive-general using coverage, persistence, future-consistency and future-action metrics plus manual audit and a logistic classifier
question: Do world-action models change robot behavior and internal representations in ways that matter for control, beyond what task success shows, compared with direct VLAs?
key_findings: LIBERO success is similar for most models (Cosmos 98.0, LingBot-VA 98.0, VLA-JEPA 97.1, pi0.5 96.6, X-VLA 95.8, FastWAM 95.3; pi0 66.9), but WAMs generally have lower jerk and boundary jumps (e.g. LingBot-VA boundary jump 0.153 vs pi0.5 0.298 and pi0 0.666) (Table 1).
WAMs tend to show stronger target-object progress and less distractor disturbance than VLAs; auxiliary WAMs sit in between (Table 2, qualitative summary in text).
Inference cost: WAM p50 latency 956-4701 ms vs 100-329 ms for VLAs (Table 3).

On RoboTwin2.0, pi0.5 looks smoother (jerk 0.022 vs LingBot-VA 0.036) but succeeds far less (44.3% vs 81.6%) and 53.0% of its episodes are low-motion failures; 95.3% of its failed episodes are stalls (Table 4, App. C.1).

SAE feature classes (Table 5): VLA features are almost never labeled predictive (pi0 0.8% current / 0.5% action; pi0.5 1.2% / 0.8%; X-VLA 0.3% / 0.9%), while LingBot-VA's future stream is 53.2% predictive and VLA-JEPA's action stream 59.8% (of only 92 active features).
Many SAE dictionaries are largely dead in some streams (e.g. FastWAM future 94.0% dead, VLA-JEPA action 91.0%, pi0.5 action 88.2%).
Authors state explicitly that the link between predictive features and object-level behavior is associative, not causal.

evidence.scale: episode counts per model not clearly reported in the parts read; public checkpoints
evidence.statistics: no: point estimates, no CIs or tests

causal_validation: None. No feature ablation or steering; the paper says its evidence is associative.
closed_loop: Behavioral metrics come from closed-loop rollouts; SAE analyses are offline on recorded latents.
limitations_stated: SAE feature labels are weak probabilistic annotations.
Object-state metrics depend on decoded traces being available.
Simulation only and public checkpoints only; WAMs have high runtime cost.
critique: A useful reminder for the review that smoothness metrics can be misleading (stalled failures look smooth), and that success-saturated benchmarks hide behavioral differences.

The memorized / reactive / predictive taxonomy is defined by the authors' own heuristics and a classifier trained on their manual audit labels; it is not validated by intervention, so 'predictive features' may simply be features from streams that are trained to predict the future.

Comparing SAE statistics across models with very different architectures, layers and dead-feature rates (up to 94%) is fragile; small active-feature counts (e.g. 92 for VLA-JEPA action) make percentages unstable.
The pi0 checkpoint underperforms on LIBERO (66.9%), which may reflect setup rather than the model family.
No numbers on how many episodes underlie each metric, so differences between models cannot be assessed for noise.
one_line: Comparing three VLAs and four world-action models on LIBERO and RoboTwin, the paper finds WAMs move more smoothly and target objects more selectively at 3-20x higher latency, and their SAE features look more future-predictive than VLA features, but all evidence is correlational.
